types.name: Screening and assessments* of potential uses of genetic resources
types.definition: identify areas and potential genetic resources, or provide the rules and guidelines for doing the research considering Indigenous Peoples and local communities*, women and youth as necessary Note: For more generic research see 2.04 Scientific Research
types.examples: research, exchange of information at different levels, policy/regulation development

types.name: Implement relevant conventions
types.definition: here related to the relevant provisions under the Convention on Biological Diversity, the High Seas Treaty (also Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction treaty or BBNJ agreement) and the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA). Note: For Nagoya Protocol see section 1.04 instead For agrobiodiversity related matters with ITPGRFA, see 9.01.12
types.examples: Designation of National Focal Points (NFP)*, participation in convention-related meetings, information exchange, implement or scale up corresponding activities, consultations, monitor and evaluate the implementation of the commitments and adjust implementation as necessary

types.name: Legislation, regulation and enforcement of bioprospecting*
types.definition: establish clear rules for assessing and accessing the genetic resources for all types of actors, as well as for the negotiation/permitting process; risk* and impact assessment* of the legislation; considering Indigenous and local communities' customary laws, protocols and procedures
types.examples: adoption and implementation of laws, regulations and other binding agreements

types.name: Capacity-building*, financial support and engagement for rights holders* and stakeholders*
types.definition: includes Indigenous Peoples and local communities*, as well as the public institution involved and the private sector
types.examples: Support for trainings, meetings, provision of information (including translation),

types.name: Free, prior, informed consent (FPIC)* before and during use of genetic resources
types.definition: before accessing and during the use of genetic resources related to Indigenous Peoples or applying their traditional knowledge* related to genetic resources Note: for all FPIC beyond ABS refer to 5.03.06 (in 5 BD Planning and Finance - 5.03 Biodiversity coordination and management)
types.examples: consultation, information materials, meetings, support for indigenous organisations, providing materials, access to legal systems

types.name: Assessment of existing and potential future mechanism
types.examples: research, exchange of information at different levels, evaluation

types.name: Establishment of relevant public bodies, including local governance institutions
types.examples: preparation, setting-up and managing the relevant public bodies

types.name: Implementation of contractual arrangements, including the issuance of permits and certification systems, while respecting the rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities* (as rightsholder* and/or indigenous business)
types.definition: defining and establishing the Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT)*, based on consultation of the different parties, issuing and controlling permits and certificates for commercial/non-commercial use e.g. for plant genetic material the Standard Material Transfer Agreement (SMTA)*
types.examples: e.g. support/ coordinate negotiations between provider, user and state

types.name: Support and control implementation
types.examples: e.g. providing support for dispute resolution, establish legal mechanisms and capacitate the persons in the judicial system.

types.name: Assessment of existing and potential future mechanism
types.examples: research, exchange of information at different levels

types.name: Establishment of relevant public bodies, including local governance institutions
types.examples: preparation, setting-up and managing the relevant public bodies

types.name: Implementation of benefit-sharing mechanisms, including controls to prevent abuses
types.definition: benefit might be monetary or non-monetary, includes development of policies and protocols for benefit transfers, monitoring of receipt of benefits, controls and evaluation Note: General access to non-financial resources are part of 5.08.02
types.examples: adoption and implementation of laws, regulations and other binding agreements, training for police and monitoring institutions, regular controls, travel, legal access for all rights holders and stakeholders*

types.name: Development of (finance) instruments to facilitate transfers of benefits to communities, including Indigenous Peoples and local communities* and women
types.definition: development of policies and protocols for benefit transfers, coordination with finance institutions, monitoring of receipt of benefits Note: General access to financial resources are part of 5.08.01
types.examples: protocols, cash transfer, controls, surveys

types.name: Ratification process of Nagoya Protocol
types.examples: sign and ratify the Nagoya Protocol; participate in convention-related meetings, information exchange, adopt the relevant legislation accordingly, implement or scale up corresponding activities, monitor and evaluate the implementation of the commitments and adjust implementation as necessary

types.name: Establishment of national focal points (NFP)*, the competent national authorities (CNA)* and, if required, national authorized users (NAU)*.
types.examples: preparation, setting-up and managing the institutions, preparing and adopting law, prepare reports, collect information, establish processes

types.name: Design and establish relevant checkpoints for implementation
ABS Clearing House Mechanism (ABSCH)
types.examples: e.g. cost of notification, reports

types.name: Awareness raising about Nagoya Protocol and ABS
types.definition: Part of communication, education and awareness (CEPA)* efforts, incl. campaigns and public information Note: for general Awareness Raising see Category 2 Awareness - Knowledge
types.examples: prepare/planning media campaigns, stakeholder* analysis, preparation of information materials, libraries, museums, excursion, advertisement

types.name: Support compliance of Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT)*
types.examples: conduct FPIC*, provide legal support, adopt legislation, monitoring and evaluation,

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* for providers, users and state-employees
types.definition: Note: For details related to learning and trainings OR if topics are broader, see 2.02 informal education (2.02.04 and 2.02.05)
types.examples: needs assessments, preparation of training material, travel, meetings between rights holders*, stakeholders* and institutions, renting spaces

types.name: Biodiversity education plan
types.definition: Strategic document prepared with educators and all relevant rights holders* and stakeholders*, including Indigenous Peoples and local communities*, women and youth that describes all education programs aiming to increase understanding of biodiversity, measure to protect and restore it and to address biodiversity loss drivers;
types.examples: may include planning, meetings, workshops, coordination, rights holders and stakeholder engagement, written materials, publications, consultants, etc.

types.name: (Pre-)primary/secondary education curriculum, development incorporating biodiversity
types.definition: Input or inclusion of biodiversity related content into the curriculum across all relevant subjects, not only in natural sciences, of pre-primary, primary schools and secondary school, and teaching of those contents or providing relevant training to teachers. It should contain not only biodiversity itself, but also the social, economic and cultural causes for biodiversity loss and the possibilities for transition to a nature-friendly future. The education should enable the acquisition of new skills.
types.examples: Includes learning materials, Teacher’s presentations&tool kits, discussions, group work, games, debates, roleplays; Production and publication of relevant educational material (text- or video-based), renumeration for teacher/trainer (if biodiversity component is clearly identificable)

types.name: Biodiversity in higher education curriculum
types.definition: Input or inclusion of biodiversity related content into existing courses, creation of new cources across all relevant subjects, not only in natural sciences, and teaching of those contents for all types of higher education or providing relevant training to teachers and professors. It should contain not only biodiversity itself, but also the social, economic and cultural causes for biodiversity loss and the possibilities for transition to a nature-friendly future.
types.examples: includes learning materials, Teacher’s presentations& tool kits, discussions, group work, games, debates, roleplays; Production and publication of relevant educational material (text- or video-based), renumeration for teacher/trainer (if biodiversity component is clearly identificable)

types.name: a) Introduction and teaching of Biodiversity protection and restoration
types.definition: see main line 2.01.03

types.name: b) Introduction and teaching of pollution, Invasive Alien Species, Genetic Modified Organism;
types.definition: see main line 2.01.03

types.name: c) Introduction and teaching of Green Economy (with BD relevance) and Sustainable Use
types.definition: see main line 2.01.03

types.name: d) Introduction and teaching of ABS
types.definition: see main line 2.01.03

types.name: e) Introduction and teaching of BD planning, finance, cooperation and communication
types.definition: see main line 2.01.03

types.name: Vocational training in tertiary level
types.definition: focusing on reaching ecological limits and for all kind of biodiversity loss drivers, analyzing the potential of hazards, the areas exposure to pollution or an accident and the vulnerability of the ecosystem (e.g. risk assessments* for biodiversity threats), vocational training could include sustainable tourism guide programs, sustainable entrepreneurhip, rangers program
types.examples: includes learning materials, Teacher’s presentations&tool kits, discussions, group work, games, debates, roleplays; Production and publication of relevant educational material (text- or video-based), renumeration for teacher/trainer

types.name: Excursions by educational institutions related to protect biodiversity (or prevent biodiversity loss drivers) relevant sites
types.definition: included here if integral part of the curriculum. Otherwise, see following subcategory Non-formal biodiversity education.
types.examples: e.g. visiting protected areas, IAS removal, coastal clean up etc... ; on the job training experience,

types.name: Inclusion of indigenous knowledge*, language and customs related to biodiversity within the national curriculum
types.definition: Recognizing and embedding the indigenous knowledge within school, vocational trainings and universities, allowing intergenerational transmission of knowledge (based on their consent)

types.name: Operation of library, archives and museums, including the preservation and exhibition of the objects/sites
types.definition: Includes supporting and operating work of museums, libraries, and etc. to support biodiversity and nature conservation-related research, management and policy; they also support public education about biodiversity
types.examples: operational and administration costs, personal, exhibition material

types.name: Excursions and time outside in nature for educational purposes outside the formal education system
types.definition: often considered as ‘experiential’ or ‘authentic’ learning
types.examples: Includes for example versatile field trips, visits to museums, and various ways of outdoor learning.

types.name: Education offers for students (school and university) beyond the curriculum and relevant training for the teachers
types.definition: Activities and input directed to local students; It could include community-based learnings, intergenerational dialogues and transmission of traditional knowledge* or be more skill-focussed
types.examples: May include education materials, audio‑visual content, meetings, etc and workshops for teachers focused on certain topics.

types.name: Technical training and advisory services to public institutions, NGOs, private companies and local communities
types.definition: Activities include advise on more sustainable practices, foster the transfer of knowledge between science and practitioners or between different practitioners and acquisition of new or enhancing already existing skills, including, but not limited to, data generation and interpretation, mapping, ... related to generic or broad biodiversity-related topics Note: topic-specific technical trainings are within the relevant Category/Subcategory
types.examples: includes learning materials, workshop costs; Production and publication of relevant educational material (text- or video-based), renumeration for teacher/trainer (if biodiversity component is clearly identificable)

types.name: Lifelong learning / Adult education* offers / Capacity-building*
types.definition: Includes all learning opportunities on the job (for vocational training itself, see 2.01.04), and not-job related offers; for re-skilling, fostering the transfer from science to practice. It could include community-based learnings, intergenerational dialogues and transmission of traditional knowledge* or be more skill-oriented Note: topic-specific learnings are within the relevant Category/Subcategory
types.examples: may include education materials, audio‑visual content, meetings, travel, venue, workshop facilitator, translations

types.name: Promotion and enabling mutual learning
types.definition: Among individuals or organizations within one country (for cross-border see below 2.02.10), including about indigenous and local communities knowledge if so desired by them Opportunities can be facilitated both online or in person, with the aim of sharing knowledge, best practices, tools and innovations
types.examples: may include meetings, travel, facilitator/trainer expenses, material for learning and interaction,

types.name: Lessons and experience sharing between institutions, regions and/or countries
types.definition: Includes all forms of South-South or Triangular learning, participation at conferences and events, both the participation of public institutions or enabling non-public institutions to participate at such knowledge exchanges
types.examples: materials, transport, attendance costs including fees

types.name: a) Lessons and experience sharing related to biodiversity protection and restoration
types.definition: see main line 2.02.10

types.name: b) Lessons and experience sharing related to pollution, Invasive Alien Species, Genetic Modified Organism
types.definition: see main line 2.02.10

types.name: c) Lessons and experience sharing related to Green Economy (with BD relevance) and Sustainable Use
types.definition: see main line 2.02.10

types.name: d) Lessons and experience sharing related to ABS
types.definition: see main line 2.02.10

types.name: e) Lessons and experience sharing related to BD planning, finance, cooperation and communication
types.definition: see main line 2.02.10

types.name: Education Workshops for decision-makers
types.definition: Activities directed to public officials and private sector leaders whose support is needed for the implementation of biodiversity measures
types.examples: May include management personnel, written materials, workshops,facilitator/trainer expenses, travel, etc.

types.name: Environmental communication and/or awareness plan
types.definition: Strategic document prepared with all relevant rights holders* and stakeholders*, including Indigenous Peoples and local communities*, women and youth that describes sets awareness/communication goals, chooses the right media and dissemination mean and key messages. One first analyses the management or biodiversity issue one wants to address. The second step is to analyse what awareness has to be generated/ communication obstacles have to be addressed to reach or change the relevant stakeholders. The third is to define for each group of stakeholders (the target group(s)) the awareness/communication objectives, the messages and the means.
types.examples: may include planning, meetings, workshops, coordination, rights holders and stakeholder engagement, written materials, publications, consultants, etc.

types.name: Periodic surveys about knowledge, attitudes and perception
types.definition: In relation to biodiversity loss, or planned interventions to reduce drivers of biodiversity loss or to procted/ restore biodiversity
types.examples: Activities include screening and analysis of public media, stakeholder meetings, knowledge, attitude, practice and opinion polls, surveys, networking and engagement with scientific institutions, rights holders* and stakeholders*

types.name: (educational) Material (text-, audio or video-based)
types.definition: To raise awareness of or inform target groups about drivers of biodiversity loss and/or possibilities to proctect/restore biodiversity, as well as to explain relevant biodiversity friendly policy changes and advocating for the necessary changes due to those policy changes. Topics include: function and value of biodiversity, its protection, root causes of drivers, biodiversity finance, governance, etc
types.examples: Production, including research, consultations, the use of photography, radio, arts, visualization, design, planning, adaptation to the different target audiences and publication, including printing, dissemination, translation, etc

types.name: Production of easy understandable, up-to-date, accurate and relevant information with open access
types.definition: Information should be provided by all actors, public, private, from science; be easily accessible (e.g. on products, at the entrance to certain areas, related websites, etc) and should explain and convey information for training, technology, experience and know-how exchange with the objective to raise awareness of or inform target groups about drivers of biodiversity loss and/or possibilities to proctect/ restore biodiversity, biodiversity finance, governance, etc
types.examples: Information provision, storage and dissemintion, e.g. web-portals, databases, physically (e.g. on products, events, booklets)

types.name: Awareness raising and outreach to all kind of stakeholders, including general public, policy makers, ministry staff, practitioners, etc
types.definition: = General expenditure, when no much information is available. See following lines for more specific lines (if budget information allows). Note: The awareness raising here is related to biodiversity topics in general, if it is related to specific topics of (sub)categories, see there

types.name: a) Awareness raising related to planned policies, their consequences and how to implement them
types.definition: Information include potential actions, responsible actors, possible socio-economic costs (of inaction) and the benefits of taking action by campaigns, advertisement, diffusion, ...

types.name: b) Awareness raising related to people's participation in budget planning
types.definition: consultations related to budget preparation and planning for biodiversity-relevant activities

types.name: c) Launch campaigns or movements to engender peoples participation to BD related events
types.definition: e.g. Biodiversity Days such as World Biodiversity Day (22nd May), World Environment Day (5th June), World Soil Day (5th Dec), etc
types.examples: publication, activities

types.name: d) Reporting internally (with stake-* and rightsholders*) and externally about conservation projects development, dissemination of lessons learnt and sharing of good practices
types.definition: Communication and reporting during planning, implementation, and after results have been (not) achieved, promoting contribution, exchange of knowledge and create ownership via reports, meetings and other communication channels, including translation where necessary

types.name: e) Establishment of physical spaces to encounter biodiversity in daily life
types.definition: e.g. biodiversity-rich gardens in schools or public parks Note: Library, archives and museums are part of 2.02 Non-formal and informal education
types.examples: construction, maintenance

types.name: Park / Center / Zoo visitor information and outreach
types.definition: Can include panels, visitor centers, and related documentation activities or workshops, excursions and similar interactive activities Note: For zoo conservation efforts, see 7.04.08 in 7.04 Conservation of Species

types.name: Support scientific research and research agenda of all sectoral agencies with biodiversity functions
types.definition: e.g. planning research agendas, funding calls, initiate collaboration among several actors etc

types.name: Support development and increase capacity of centers of excellence for biodiversity research and enable creation of networks and exchange among experts and practitioners
types.definition: including think tanks, laboratories
types.examples: infrastructure, equipment, set-up the center adminsitratively and physically, trainings & capacity-building*

types.name: Contribution to the Intergovernmental science-policy platform for biodiversity and ecosystem services (IPBES)*
types.definition: e.g. by nominating a focal point, support for the IPBES secretariat or contributors to the assessments, attendance of IPBES meetings Note: Research itself is part of the lines below in this subcategory 2.04
types.examples: travel, venue, provide the means for experts to participate in the assessemts, share data, etc

types.name: Research related to harmonized methods and protocols to collect, process and exchange data, and develop, harmonize, measure and incorporate purposeful biodiversity indicators* and definitions
types.definition: Establish sustainable (long-term useful) methods that allow comparisons, collaboration and exchange; as well as purposeful indicators to measure biodiversity trends and the ecosystem functions. for Biodiversity Indicator Development Framework see e.g. https://www.bipindicators.net/national-indicator-development/bidf
types.examples: research based on literature, key-experts, data-reviews and field studies, comparing available data and methods, visualization and mainstreaming options (e.g. maps, models)

types.name: Collection, processing, hosting and storing of data related to biodiversity
types.definition: Activities include biodiversity-relevant qualitative and quantitative (big) data collection in order to increase the efficiency, determine best practices, prepare feasibility studies, etc contributing to biodiversity research Data can be collected via observation, photography and analysis, digital tools as e.g. satelite or georeferenced information systems Digitalize and share data, use and enhance databases
types.examples: Equipment, infrastructure, maintenance for collection, storage and exchange of the data and its accessibility

types.name: Risk frameworks and mitigation strategies
types.definition: focusing on reaching ecological limits and for all kind of biodiversity loss drivers, analyzing the potential of hazards, the areas exposure to pollution or an accident and the vulnerability of the ecosystem (e.g. risk assessments* for biodiversity threats due to agriculture activity, specific pollutants, overuse) or to ensure prevention measures (e.g. disaster risk reduction, protected area management) Note: Risk assessments themselves are integrated within the subcategories, usually within the Conservation Management Plans or Strategy Assessment.

types.name: Scientific research aiming to benefit biodiversity
types.definition: = General expenditure, when no much information is available. See following lines for more specific (if budget information allows). In all cases includes research carried out by public entities or the support e.g. in form of grants to scholar or research institutions, NGOs and private entities

types.name: a) Basic research and experimental development on natural sciences, engineering, social sciences
types.definition: Experimental or theoretical work mostly focusing on the foundations of a field without any foreseen particular application or use, but with links to biodiversity (e.g. biology, behavioral science, water, ...)
types.examples: administration and operation of agencies focused on research, financial support for non-governmental bodies (think tanks, universities, ...)

types.name: b) Fundamental research and gap analysis related to measuring biodiversity change
types.definition: Activities for fundamental research include defining major research gaps, research about methods, assessments*, taxonomy, genetics, indicators* and scalability. Biodiversity has many dimensions including variety, quantity, composition and distribution.
types.examples: develop and measure indicators of the state of biodiversity on regional, national and international level, including e.g. species inventories; generation, discovery, capture, management and use of biodiversity-related data, information and knowledge

types.name: c) Screening and assessments* of current situations and likely trends, as well as assessment of ecological limits, ecosystem impact monitoring
types.definition: Includes especially the identification of key biodiversity hotspots*, conservation status intervention areas and scalable measures, Ecological limits for a healthy ecosystem, e.g. as defined with the planetary boundaries*
types.examples: It may involve reviewing scientific and grey literature, include key experts, monitor datasets

types.name: d) Pilot studies
types.definition: Includes the perspective of theory and method, opportunities to test and advance hypothesized tendencies toward environmental improvement through assessment of material practices and organizational strategies

types.name: e) Research on alternative practices and materials that put less pressure on biodiversity or increase biodiversity
types.definition: Includes the development or transfer of technology

types.name: f) Research opportunities for biodiversity with digitalization and integration of relevant tools, including computer software, apps, Artifical Inteligence (AI) to contribute to any of the above mentioned research activities or to conserve/restore biodiversity
types.definition: Includes the transfer, adaptation and development of tools for biodiversity purposes

types.name: g) Research regarding risks and opportunities related to biotechnology
types.definition: includes in particular the associated risks for rights holders* and stakeholders*
types.examples: research based on literature, key-experts, data-reviews and field studies,

types.name: h) Preservation and research with museum projects and documentation
Genetic sequencing
types.definition: Gene sequencing is a new way to identify, characterize, manage, and monitor species by e.g. by providing better understanding of genetic variability in species populations Note: Any measure related to access and benefit sharing derived due to genetic sequencing, see 1 ABS

types.name: Monetary and non-monetary valuation of Biodiversity and ecosystems
types.definition: for national level, e.g. with the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)* or for specific sites and projects, e.g with Transfer Valuation Methods, Cultural Assessment Methods, Nature's Contribution Concept
types.examples: Incorparate environmental data, the environmental national assets (stocks) and flows in the national accounting system

types.name: Documentation, dissemination and exchange of lessons learnt and best practices
types.definition: support the compilation of information with different public, private and civil actors, both within and between different regions and states

types.name: Assessments*, Monitoring and Evaluations, as e.g. Impact and Strategic assessments* (ex-ante or post), rapid ecological assessments, period and long-term reviews before/after implementing new laws or projects
types.definition: Impact Assessments involves a process of evaluating the likely impacts, both beneficial and adverse, of a proposed development on the ecosystem, habitat, cultural landscape or other relevant area and the resulting socio-cultural consequences. The assessments needs to take cumulative impacts into account, when appropriate.
types.examples: Assessments includes the research based on literature, key-experts, data-reviews and field studies.

types.name: Promotion and enabling citizen science*
types.definition: Citizen science is the involvement of the public in scientific research – whether community-driven research or global investigations. States can provide financial and non-financial resources, raise awareness, provide (access to) data Can be related to all types of biodiversity topics.
types.examples: includes training, capacity-building*, providing plattforms, raising awareness

types.name: Promotion of participatory and gender-responsive transdisciplinary approaches and co-creation of knowledge within the biodiversity field
types.definition: Note: For inclusion of indigenous or traditional knowledge*, see subcategory below: 2.05 Indigenous and local community knowledge

types.name: Develop protocols and community plans in close collaboration with Indigenous Peoples and local communities
types.definition: e.g. Biocultural Community Protocols (BCPs)* for Nagoya, community plans for livelihood, co-management of (protected) areas based to establish clear terms of collaboration and cooperation

types.name: Support for an assessment of the status of traditional knowledge and its level of recognition and inclusion in policy and management
types.definition: Review to assess the conceptual, operational and implementation inclusion as baseline analysis Important to support as required by the Indigenous Peoples and local communities

types.name: Integration of indigenous knowledges* and practices and full and effective participation of Indigenous Peoples and local communities into decision making
types.definition: Promoting inclusive governance approaches through rights holders* and stakeholder* engagement while deciding/implementing biodiversity-friendly management practices (see e.g. Sustainable Use), including the use of traditional management practices associated with Indigenous Peoples and local communities; for green economy, when developing new projects in their territories (based on their consent)

types.name: Bio-cultural protocols
Support for community-led local development strategies
types.definition: with Indigenous Peoples and local community members using, sharing, preserving their knowledge according to their judgement; by collaboration of traditional knowledge and science working on multiple-benefit solution, including for biodiversity, e.g. for area management, domestication of medicinal plants, sustainable use, trainings, partnerships in communal libraries, developing technologies to generate a commercial natural product

types.name: Co-generation of data, research and knowledge
types.definition: Includes for example data about medicinal plants, additional food sources, agriculture/hunting/sampling methods excludes: linguistic research (unless traditional plants vocabulary)

types.name: Research on impacts on traditional knowledge and socio-cultural practices
types.definition: conserving, documenting and providing learning opportunities for the traditional knowledge, valorisation within and outside the education system

types.name: Safeguard traditional knowledge* and support its preservation
types.definition: based on their needs and consent, includes collection and documentation of this knowledge, supporting them with organization, documentation and identify needs for their resilience (e.g. assessed by using the "community viability framework" as developed by UNEP WCMC)
types.examples: e.g. providing the infrastructure, server, capacity-building* based on the needs and requests of the Indigenous Peoples and local communities

types.name: Free, prior, informed consent (FPIC)* before any research about or use of indigenous knowledge
types.definition: Inclusion of indigenous knowledge within FPIC processes, and realizing an FPIC before using their knowledge Note: for all FPIC beyond indigenous knowledge refer to 5.03.06 (in 5 BD Planning and Finance - 5.03 Biodiversity coordination and management)
types.examples: consultation, information materials, meetings; and all costs associated to the preparation, formulation, negotiation, adoption and implementation of laws, regulations that guarantee/institutionalize this right

types.name: Contribution to the CBD website or any of the priority activities established by the CBD
types.definition: as agreed in decision 31 at COP11: UNEP/CBD/COP/11/31

types.name: Establishment of a global biodiversity knowledge network
types.definition: Combining already existing information from organisations, initiatives and processes; promote and facilitate coordination, collaboration, interconnection and networking among those knowledge management entities with a view to making biodiversity data and information and knowledge more readily available and accessible for biodiversity planning, policy and decision‑making, implementation, monitoring, reporting and review

types.name: Establishment of national and regional focal points and other bodies as relevant to monitor the CBD implementation progress
types.examples: preparation, setting-up and managing the relevant focal points and institutions

types.name: Preparation of NBSAPs, national reports and other requested information
types.examples: Collect, classify and prepare the information regarding the progress of the targets based on the indicators* and implementation of other decisions taken at the CBD COPs

types.name: Participation in voluntary peer reviews
types.examples: By providing the relevant data, assess/provide feedback to other countries progress

types.name: Identification and prioritization of IAS species, their introduction pathways and most effective measures to avoid direct or indirect introduction and their impacts
types.definition: Identification of IAS and relevant measures can be determined by scientific research (see also 2.04 Biodiversity Scientific Research). For the prioritization, the local and most effected persons should be effectively included. Relevant standards for analysing IAS are: - Environmental Impact Classification for Alien Taxa (EICAT) http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/about_eicat.php - CITES can be used to analyse the risk of an IAS for endangered species
types.examples: Information exchange at regional and global levels

types.name: Invasive Alien Species Management Plan
types.definition: Baseline analysis, risk assessment* and management, focusing on introduction and impact on the affected ecosystems, identification of measures for prevention, mitigation and recovery, monitoring, involving rights holders* and stakeholders*
types.examples: may include planning, meetings, workshops, coordination, stakeholder engagement, written materials, publications, consultants, etc.

types.name: Assessments*, Monitoring and Evaluations, as e.g. Impact and Strategic assessments (ex-ante or post), rapid ecological assessments, period and long-term reviews
types.definition: focus on early IAS detection*, horizon scanning, the impact of IAS, main entry pathways and potential responses Note: For more generic research on baselines, see 2.04 Scientific Research; for data collection using citizen science see 2.04.12

types.name: Prevention of entry between and within states
types.definition: part of pathway management: apply precautionary principle before releasing alien species (e.g. for food production), definition/implementation of standards, cooperation across states, etc. including relevant trainings and controls Note: all measures related to the border itself, see below 3.01.05
types.examples: Improve information dissemination and trade negotiations, controls, border staff, quarantine maintenance

types.name: Border control, including sanitary measures and quarantine
types.definition: part of pathway management: Ensure border control facility and quarantine capacity to be in place and their maintainance and apply sanitary and phytosanitary measures on trade goods and commodity.
types.examples: Infrastructure, equipment for detection / setting up protocols for detection, reporting and quick action

types.name: Management / removal of coastal and marine debris
types.examples: labour costs, equipment, handling and disposal facilities

types.name: Eradication of already entered species
types.definition: Removal of species with lethal and non-lethal means, including sterilization and breeding restrictions or necessary condition for living (i.e. ant nests), including the necessary Cost Benefit analysis
types.examples: Physical removal through chemical or manual means, including hunting

types.name: Containment and long-term control measures
types.definition: e.g. fences or nets
types.examples: Manual or chemical interventions; enforcement of land use plans including segregation of IAS areas

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* for border and control staff and institutions engaged with monitoring
types.definition: Formal and non-formal training and rollout to field staff, local governments, industry stakeholders* Note: For details related to learning and trainings OR if topics are broader, see 2.02 informal education (2.02.04 and 2.02.05)
types.examples: Development of training materials, conference facilities, travel

types.name: Awareness raising and outreach to general public, policy makers and relevant actors
types.definition: Part of communication, education and awareness (CEPA)* efforts. With focus on policy makers, the general public and potential importers of alien species to inform about their impact on biodiversity and economy and promote e.g. codes of conduct in relation to entered species and create early detection alarms, shift values (e.g. towards native and non-invasive species) Note: for general Awareness Raising see Category 2 Awareness - Knowledge
types.examples: Mainstream / social media info campaigns, comms materials, advocacy events

types.name: Implementation of relevant conventions

types.definition: including e.g. risk assessment*, monitoring,

types.definition: Note: Only for GMO related evaluation, general risk frameworks and their mitigation are part of 2.04.06 in 2.04 Scientific Research (2 BD Awareness - Knowledge)

types.name: Measures related to trade/ use of GMOs

types.name: Setting of standards and information about handling, transport, packaging and identification of GMOs including for transboundary movement

types.name: Contribution to new/existing databases on GMO use

types.name: Raising awareness and outreach related to GMO processes and standards and potential impact on health and environment
types.definition: Facilitating informed public participation and application of the precautionary principle
types.examples: communication and outreach, interactions with stakeholders*, media campaigns, preparation of information materials

types.name: Liability mechanisms for damage-causing GMO introductions
types.definition: Mechanisms could include liability for development damage-causing risks and retroactive liability. To prevent the development of risk for GMO introduction, insurance schemes may apply. For retroactive liability, compensation schemes and funds could be established.

types.name: Compliance to international and regional and sub-regional agreements on Biosafety, in particular the Cartagena Protocol
types.definition: including establishment of relevant public bodies or focal points, adjustment of standards and procedures

types.name: Programs for monitoring and enforcement procedures for use and trade of GMO
types.definition: including e.g. compliance with law, trade controls, but also post-approval monitoring of species introduction, as a risk management technique. includes also the evaluation and control of impacts related to ecosystems, human health, economic development, traditional knowledge* and socio-cultural practices.
types.examples: Documentation, information verification, training and capacity-building*

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* for teachers and facilitators, media, private sectors, traders/users, civil society organizations etc.
types.definition: Note: For details related to learning and trainings OR if topics are broader, see 2.02 informal education (2.02.04 and 2.02.05)
types.examples: Development of training materials, conference facilities, travel

types.name: Transparent and accurate provision of information of biodiversity impacts along the supply chain or legislation encouraging such information
types.definition: Reporting/data or legislation encourage such information, e.g. information on agricultural commodities (soya, beef, palm oil, etc), timber, raw materials or others on how such commodities are produced, traded and consumed. Note: the suggested rating here is if the supply chain expenditure is explicitly related to biodiversity; otherwise the BD Attribution rate should be significant lower

types.name: Incentives and regulation for green supply chain leading towards a circular economy
types.definition: Focusing on reduced use of resources, sustainably sourced, by increased reuse of materials and products improved logistics and increased efficiency E.g. The EU adopted the new circular economy action plan with legislative and non-legislative measures, focus on the sectors that use most resources and where the potential for circularity is high such as: electronics and ICT, batteries and vehicles, packaging, plastics, textiles, construction and buildings, food, water and nutrients.
types.examples: Implementation of laws, regulations and incentives, including their control and enforcement

types.name: Disclosure of environmental impact, exposure to environmental risks and opportunities

types.definition: via information campaigns, internal policies, incentives Note: For biodiversity-friendly procurement, see 4.03.03 below

types.definition: e.g. ban of certain products due to biodiversity concerns during the sourcing, requiring certain standards Note: trade legislation aiming to avoid invasive alien species are in 3.01 (Biosafety)

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* to reduce biodiversity harm along the supply chain
types.definition: Note: For details related to learning and trainings OR if topics are broader, see 2.02 informal education (2.02.04 and 2.02.05)

types.name: Development and monitoring of progressive taxation policy
types.definition: e.g. Price-based royalties, which are production-based royalties with rates varying according to mineral prices. Examples: Côte d’Ivoire, Bolivia; e.g. Operating profit ratio based royalties, which are production-based royalties with rates varying according to the ratio of operating profit to gross revenue. Examples: South Africa, Niger.; e.g. Operating profit taxes, which are based on various definitions of operating profits and with rates varying according to the ratio of operating profit to gross revenue. Examples: Chile, Peru.
types.examples: policy and economic research, consultations

types.name: Disclosure of environmental impact by extractive activities and mitigation measures taken
types.definition: Harmonization of national standards, provision of incentives and control mechanisms to ensure disclosure of those environmental impacts caused by public or private economic activity, including mitigation measures taken. Reporting should be based on Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA)*, in particular before new infrastructure or sourcing project. Companies and business can be also guided by the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)*.
types.examples: travel, venue, training material, workshop facilitator, translations

types.name: Earmarking / Retention of revenues generated from extractives
types.definition: e.g. export or inland selling of raw material or (semi-) processed goods; to be considered as biodiversity- friendly the retained revenues need to be clearly earmarked for biodiversity protection includes green jobs*, social protection of vulnerable groups, restoration, maintenance etc Ex: Philippines ' DENR Administrative Order 2022-04, Enhancing Biodiversity Conservation and Protection in Mining Operations provide adequate measures for responsible mining towards ensuring biodiversity conservation and protection including progressive and final rehabilitation of mined-out areas. Potentially, this policy may be able to redirect 50% of fund commitments by mining companies to biodiversity conservation.

types.name: Green investment plan for the sector
types.examples: Planning, preparation, defining goals, establishing clear criteria, map investment opportunities, identifying legal gaps, implement monitoring and evaluation

types.name: Enforcement of mining regulations including EIA* provisions
types.definition: e.g. limited exploration in certain areas, ensuring financing of restoration activities, minimized environmental impacts during construction, use of alternative methods/technologies for exploration/mining, licensing, environmental permitting, applying biodiversity offsets mechanism (avoid/minimize/restore/offset)

types.name: Measures to avoid or reduce biodiversity impact during extractive process
types.definition: new/improved technology, avoiding certain areas, etc measures should be informed by EIA* enforced/incentivized e.g. financial subsidies, enforcement of regulations, access to infrastructure, information campaigns, …
types.examples: Implementation of incentives, including the monitoring and evaluation of their effectiveness and follow-up actions, information material

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* to reduce biodiversity harm during operation and related to biodiversity compensation schemes

types.name: Assessment of ecological limits for (sustainable) production and consumption
types.definition: Develop, harmonize, measure and incorporate indicators*, measure and analyse relevant data, agree on harmonized methods, exchange of information among all relevant actors; including traditional knowledge* with free, prior, informed consent (FPIC)* of Indigenous Peoples Note: Limits for sectors related to productive areas and/or species, such as agriculture, forestry and fisheries are covered in the relevant subcategory in 9 Sustainable Use, here it focuses on limits related to production (consumption of energy, manufacturing) or tourism for ex..

types.name: Specialized product design to optimize the product in a biodiversity friendly way (e.g. less resources)
types.definition: e.g. already considering reuse and repair options, consider material sources Examples: CAMIF Conso’ localization service: the consumer can choose online the equipment item of his/her house (furniture, bedding …) according to the proximity of the place of production to his/her home. This allows the decrease of CO2 emissions at the delivery stage and is a good example of an aspect of the eco-design approach implemented by the manufacturer. IKEA’s Kungsbacka kitchen is also made from recycled plastic bottles and wood Note: Changes related to Reduction of Pollution (Protection of soil, water, air, waste management, and other) of any kind, are considered within 6 Pollution Management
types.examples: Legislation, controls and enforcement of established rules in this area; standard setting

types.name: Biodiversity-friendly public procurement procedures
types.definition: Example: Slovenia’s National Action Plan on GPP covers the period 2009-2012. It sets a target for 50% of all procurement by central government authorities in eight product groups to include GPP criteria by 2012. For electricity, the target is 100% green procurement, reflecting the availability of hydroelectric and biomass (wood) energy sources. The strategy also includes training on GPP, pilot projects and assisting public authorities in attaining third-party certified environmental management systems.
types.examples: Awareness, change of guidelines, capacity-building*, training, pilot projects

types.name: Incentives or legislation to increase the reuse of material and products, including their repair or second-hand sale
types.definition: E.g. The EU adopted the new circular economy action plan with legislative and non-legislative measures, focus on the sectors that use most resources and where the potential for circularity is high such as: electronics and ICT, batteries and vehicles, packaging, plastics, textiles, construction and buildings, food, water and nutrients. It introduces legislative and non-legislative measures targeting areas where action at the EU level brings real added value. Note: Measures solely focusing on Waste Management, can be found in 6.03 Waste Management
types.examples: Implementation of laws, regulations and incentives, including their control

types.name: Disclosure of environmental impact regarding the whole life-cycle of products
types.definition: Establish national standards, support relevant research, provide information portals Note: For more generic research see 2.04 Scientific Research
types.examples: research, media campaigns, design

types.name: Incentives for optimal resource use (e.g. water use)
types.definition: Nudges and incentives, for example progressive prices on natural resources use, e.g. water, energy, etc; with the objective to reduce resource use and pressure on biodiversity

types.name: Earmarking / Investment of rents generated from financial mechanisms in green jobs*, social protection of vulnerable groups

types.name: Innovative energy systems not harming (or even supporting) biodiversity conservation
types.definition: E.g. projects that combines offshore wind farms with fish stock regeneration, specific well adapted hydropower plants, wind turbines detecting birds, …

types.name: Non-extractive practices* of wildlife use
types.definition: Includes the promotion for non-extractive practices (e.g. nature observation and photography), as well as measures to reduce impact of nature-based tourism on wildlife (e.g., measures includes time limits (seasonal or daytime), reducing stress, min distance rules, education and training programs) etc Note: all other sustainable wildlife use is within 9.09
types.examples: Observation infrastructure, educational material, control, guides

types.name: Marketing and promotion of biodiversity related to tourism
types.definition: promotion of natural sites, specific species, ecosystem and the biodiversity-compatible activities, including by media campaigns, libraries, museums, excursion, advertisement

types.name: Overall management, protection and development of natural heritage tourism
types.definition: Heritage tourism refers to areas with historical, cultural or natural significance and often involves local communities and their cultural activities. Natural heritage might entails specific landscapes, ecosystems or geological formations with activities such as nature walks or safaris.

types.definition: e.g. from nature-based tourism; expenditures related to ensure the tourism services that generates the revenue can be considered when revenues are clearly earmarked for biodiversity protection includes green jobs*, social protection of vulnerable groups, restoration, maintenance etc

Companies and business can be also guided by the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)*.

types.name: Incentives and planning for biodiversity friendly transport options or making transport as biodiversity-friendly as possible
types.definition: e.g. avoiding harm by considering biodiversity concerns in design and planning phase (going for the lowest BD impact), e.g. avoiding key biodiversity areas (protected areas and others), providing incentives to reduce the harm of the transport in place (e.g. by addressing security of crossing, noise or toxic pollution, land use change, deforestation, the use of ice-melting salt, etc) Examples: planning that includes wildlife needs in the design, economic incentives as tax incentives, loan programs, guarantees, and credit, e.g. for ensuring passage (bridges/tunnels) for animals across transport infrastructure
types.examples: planning, field studies, construction, material costs

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* to reduce biodiversity harm for infrastructure and logistics
types.definition: Note: For details related to learning and trainings OR if topics are broader, see 2.02 informal education (2.02.04 and 2.02.05) For transport planning refer to 4.07.05
types.examples: travel, venue, training material, workshop facilitator, translations

types.definition: limited to measures that benefit biodiversity, e.g. green infrastructure, nature-based solutions* including for water basins (not the chlorification, chemical treatment etc for drinking water) Note: all general measures related to prevent or reduce pollution are in 6.01 Protection and remediation of soil, groundwater and surface water

types.name: Biodiversity-friendly infrastructure (buildings, utility projects and other civil engineering projects)
types.definition: Refers to both the reduction of biodiversity impacts and providing benefits by applying biodiversity consideration during the planning face of or changes to existing infrastructure, including the maintenance of those spaces, e.g. by transitioning from grey to green infrastructure, or small-scale improvements (e.g. creating nesting spots, adopted colours, green roofs), change in the set-up of the project to reduce threats to species (e.g. location and design of powerlines),

types.name: Disaster risk reduction
types.definition: Risk assessment* (hazard, exposure, vulnerability) and reduction via e.g. green infrastructure, nature-based solutions*. Note: only measures with co-benefit (e.g. improvement of areas to guarantee certain ecosystem areas) should be considered here. Measures that use biodiversity, but have no biodiversity objective are not eligible. Note 2: Only for inhabitated areas (for unhabitated areas see 7.02.07 in protection of areas outside of PA)

types.name: Lifelong learning, technical training & capacity-building* to include biodiversity into planning and local processes (e.g. procurement, construction, etc) and infrastructure

types.name: Change of existing or Creation of new laws to protect or restore biodiversity, ensure its sustainable use, guarantee access and benefit sharing and address all drivers of biodiversity loss
types.definition: Formulation, evaluation and required changes for all laws related to any of the 9 Biodiversity Categories, e.g. creating the legal framework for ABS, mechanisms to reduce pollution harmful for biodiversity, laws to repurpose harmful subsidies, protection of forests or wildlife in-situ, etc Note: The execution of those laws is within the relevant category.
types.examples: expert consultation, stakeholder* meetings, legal opinions

types.name: Harmonization of (inter-)national standards, analysis and disclosure of environmental impact by companies and public projects
types.definition: Incentives and regulations that increase the use of national standards for the analysis and disclosures. Companies and business can be also guided by the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD)*, respecting the free, prior, informed consent (FPIC)* for Indigenous People.

types.name: Measures to safeguard biodiversity and ecosystem services by financial institutions, business, public institutions and other relevant actors, including the civil society
types.definition: Incentives and regulation includes providing the framework for market-based approaches (e.g. credit lines, insurances, future contracts) or non-market-based (e.g. justice-based initiatives, ecosystem-based adaptation, co-management). Note: For sector-specific regulations see the specific sections, e.g. 9.04 Sustainable Fishery

types.name: Prosecution and judgement of any infringement of biodiversity-relevant law, as well as national and international biodiversity-relevant crimes
types.definition: Including the surveillance includes also seizing of financial revenues from illegal activities and illegal financing

types.name: Policy coherence and mainstreaming to include biodiversity relevant aspects in all other sector's plans, policies, regulations and decision-making processes
types.definition: Revision of laws to align with biodiversity objectives Mainstreaming biodiversity as crosscutting elements in other sectors (e.g. climate adaptation, tourism, poverty, development, economy, etc) plans and laws includes all aspects related to conservation, restoration and sustainable use by introducing safeguards, incentives for or mandatory best practices, integrated ecosystem-based approaches* and by creating synergies between the sector and biodiversity goals e.g. soil loss and soil biodiversity should not only be in laws related to agriculture and forestry (that would be part of 5.01 Biodiversity laws), but also in infrastructure, mining, energy, transport and spatial planning, promoting sustainable soil use practices

types.name: Screening of new legislation, regulation and other binding agreements for biodiversity impacts
types.definition: Evaluating the biodiversity impact of proposed legislation, including the mitigation or compensation (off-setting) of negative consequences

types.name: Framework to encourage biodiversity friendly investment and prevent harmful ones with incentives and regulation for the financial sector
types.definition: De-risking of sustainable investments and increase access to finance for a transition in favour of biodiversity Frameworks should be developed for relevant actors, including for: - holding companies - Trusts, funds and similar financial entities - Insurance and reinsurance - Pension funding - Private companies / Business activities

types.name: Prosecution and judgement of international biodiversity-relevant crimes for non-biodiversity sectors
types.definition: Including the surveillance includes also seizing of financial revenues from illegal activities and illegal financing

types.definition: Planning, preparing, adoption and updating, including all relevant stake-* and rightsholders* in the process
types.examples: Preparation, formulation, consultations implementation, its monitoring and evaluation,

types.name: Science-based monitoring* and evaluation for adaptive management
types.definition: Monitoring and evaluation of implementation and the effect of actions, legislation, etc and initiating corrective measures (e.g. change of law, action plan etc)
types.examples: Monitoring and evaluation, studies, documentation of implemented action, analysis of impacts generated, monitoring, evaluation, meeting with relevant stakeholders*

types.name: Administration, coordination and consultation among one or several state agencies or between state agencies and stakeholders*
types.definition: Includes the administration of biodiversity-related offices, including the collection of payments, bills etc earmarked and/or used for biodiversity, coordination and consultation among several administration units (e.g. Finance and Environment Ministry, or central with regional governments) and the inclusion of non-governmental stakeholders and rights holders* into the coordination processes

types.name: Support for community-based approaches and conservation*
types.definition: Enable community-based approaches and conservation* for specific areas or topics by adopting relevant legislation or policies, transferring back to communities access and use rights, transferring competences, supporting with capacity-building*, access to information and the relevant tools, as well as creating partnerships with the public and private sector actors to develop programmes for the sustainable use of a variety of natural resources.

types.name: Participation of rights holders* and stakeholders* in planning and implementation processes
types.definition: Offering opportunities for and soliciting input from rights holders and stakeholders

types.name: Free, prior, informed consent (FPIC)*
types.definition: for all biodiversity legislation and measures that effects Indigenous Peoples as set out in the International Labour Convention 169 Note: specific FPIC lines for ABS (1.01.05 within bioprospecting*), Indigenous knowledge (2.05.09), Protected Areas and other Conservation Measures (for PA and ICCA 7.01.05 and for areas outside PA and ICCA 7.02.03)
types.examples: consultation, information materials, meetings; and all costs associated to the preparation, formulation, negotiation, adoption and implementation of laws, regulations that guarantee/institutionalize this right, support for indigenous organisations, providing materials, access to legal systems

types.name: Platforms for coordination within (private/public) sector and other stakeholders* (NGOs, consumer groups)
types.definition: Provision of relevant platforms and spaces for offline/online meetings, workshops and and providing other ways to interact
types.examples: travel, venue, platform costs (server etc), specific funds allocated to stakeholders, coordination

types.name: Regional (transboundary) cooperation
types.definition: Effective cross-border cooperation, bi- or multilateral for exchanging information and data or joint action (research or implementation), capacity-building* or technology transfer; also applies across borders of different legal entities within one state
types.examples: Participation in regional meetings and information exchange, development of common quick action protocols, maintenance of databases

types.name: Protection for environmental defenders
types.definition: Ensuring the safety of environmental defenders by prevent, investigate, and punish attacks, adopt relevant law, pursue crimes and threats against environmental defenders, reduce impunity, increasing the liability of companies

types.name: Biodiversity Finance Policy and Institutional Review (PIR) at national / sub national levels
types.definition: Development, contribution, cooperation and adoption of the PIR
types.examples: analysis, research reviews, consultations, meetings
